NodeMaven is the best NetNut replacement for account-based work: its IP Quality Filter screens residential and mobile IPs before assignment, sticky sessions are long, traffic rolls over, and it sells ISP proxies from $2.99 per IP with unlimited traffic for former NetNut static users. NetNut's July 2026 seizure, after Google linked its residential exit nodes to the Popa botnet, left many customers worried not just about uptime but about IP reputation. NodeMaven's whole pitch is IP quality: every residential and mobile IP is screened before it reaches you. This page explains what happened to NetNut, compares NodeMaven with NetNut's former offer, and covers what to consider when migrating account-based and scraping workloads.
What happened to NetNut?

On July 2, 2026, the FBI, working with IRS Criminal Investigation, Google, Lumen and the Shadowserver Foundation, seized hundreds of domains tied to NetNut, the residential proxy service owned by Nasdaq-listed Alarum Technologies. Google's Threat Intelligence Group said NetNut's exit-node pool overlapped with Popa, a botnet it estimated at about two million consumer devices, many of them smart TVs and streaming boxes. Alarum disputes the botnet label and said it would cooperate with law enforcement, but netnut.com and, within days, netnut.io displayed federal seizure notices. As of October 2026 the service is not something you can responsibly buy or rely on.

blocks.text: NodeMaven in 2026: what you get

NodeMaven competes on IP quality rather than pool size. Every residential and mobile IP passes through its IP Quality Filter before it is assigned, with three strictness levels, and the company reports a 95% clean-IP rate. Proxyway's testing found the filter lowered fraud scores noticeably on sticky sessions. The pool is 30M+ residential plus 250K mobile IPs in 150+ countries, traffic rolls over, and you get up to 10% cashback on used gigabytes plus a guarantee that pays out for bad proxies.

NodeMaven is the quality-first option. Instead of handing out whatever IP the pool returns, it screens addresses in real time and lets you choose how strict the screening is. That matters most for account-based work such as social media management and multi-accounting, where a flagged IP can cost you an account. The price reflects it: $4.50/GB without a plan and $2.20/GB on monthly plans.

Strengths: IP Quality Filter screens IPs before you get them; Long sticky sessions for account work; Traffic rollover and cashback; Quality guarantee that pays for bad IPs. Weak spots: Smaller pool than mass-market networks; No datacenter proxies; Pay-as-you-go rate is double the plan rate.
What NetNut offered, and how NodeMaven compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. NodeMaven covers much of the same ground: isp proxies (from $2.99/ip), scraping browser sit alongside its residential network, which advertises 30M+ residential + 250K mobile IPs in 150+ countries.

delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, NodeMaven's answer is yes; its other products are ISP proxies (from $2.99/IP), Scraping Browser. On rotating residential targeting, NodeMaven offers country, region, city and ISP in 150+ countries, with rotating or long sticky sessions (multi-day). On billing, NodeMaven uses monthly plans or PAYG; up to 10% cashback on used traffic, and unused traffic is handled as follows: unused traffic rolls over. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
NodeMaven pricing

NodeMaven charges $4.50/GB pay-as-you-go and $2.20/GB on monthly plans, with residential and mobile traffic on one balance. A $3.50 trial includes 750 MB. Unused traffic rolls over, and you earn up to 10% cashback on used traffic. ISP proxies start at $2.99 per IP with unlimited traffic. Quick cost check for NodeMaven: 10 GB comes to $45 PAYG ($4.50/GB), and 100 GB comes to about $220 on a monthly plan ($2.20/GB). NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to NodeMaven
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to NodeMaven's targeting (country, region, city and ISP).
2. Test before you commit. NodeMaven's testing option: $3.50 trial with 750 MB. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. NodeMaven supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where NodeMaven fits best
General web scraping: workable. Why: the quality filter matters less for high-rotation crawling.
SERP and rank tracking: workable. Why: workable, but you pay a premium for filtering you may not need.
Social media and multi-account management: strong fit. Why: pre-screened, low-fraud-score IPs with long sticky sessions.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: workable. Why: fine for light checks.
Ad verification and geo-testing: workable. Why: good quality but a smaller pool.
Tight budgets: workable. Why: mid-priced on plans, expensive on PAYG.
Protocols and sessions

NodeMaven supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 and offers rotating or long sticky sessions (multi-day). Targeting covers country, region, city and ISP across 150+ countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

NetNut's customers did not choose to route traffic through a botnet; they bought what looked like a standard enterprise service. The lesson is to check sourcing before you buy, not after. Whichever provider replaces NetNut for you, NodeMaven included, run through these checks:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it.
